title: Cabernet Franc
description: Also called Bouchet in Saint-Émilion and Breton in the Loire. The aromatic parent of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.
L: Describe Cabernet Franc's flavours and structure

Cabernet Franc gives medium-bodied reds with raspberry, red currant, violet, graphite and a leafy or green pepper note. Tannins are finer and lighter than Cabernet Sauvignon's, acidity fresh. It's more aromatic and lighter, with a characteristic herbal edge.

DNA shows Cabernet Franc is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon, with Sauvignon Blanc, of Merlot, with Magdeleine Noire des Charentes, and of Carmenère. It probably came from the Basque Country. It buds and ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon, so it suits cooler places, but it still carries pyrazines, which give green notes when unripe.
Parent of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot
Which grape is Cabernet Franc a parent of?
Cabernet Franc crossed with Sauvignon Blanc to give Cabernet Sauvignon.

Look for medium ruby colour, red fruit with violet and a leafy, pencil-shaving or green pepper note. On the palate, fresh acidity and fine, medium tannins. It's lighter than Cabernet Sauvignon and less plummy than Merlot. A leafy, perfumed red with red fruit often means Cabernet Franc.
Cabernet Franc ripens later than Cabernet Sauvignon.
Not true. It ripens earlier, which is why it suits cooler places like the Loire.
Cabernet Franc gives raspberry, violet and a leafy note
It's a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Carmenère
It ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon
Loire, Bordeaux and the New World

Cabernet Franc's two French homes are the Loire, where it makes single-variety reds, and Bordeaux, where it's a blending grape, especially on the Right Bank. It also grows in the south-west. In the Loire it's sometimes called Breton; in Saint-Émilion, Bouchet.

Cabernet Franc tolerates cold winters better than Cabernet Sauvignon, and ripens earlier. That suits the Loire, northern Italy and even Canada and New York. In warmer places, like Argentina's Valle de Uco, California, Virginia and Hungary's Villány, it gives riper, fuller wines, with fewer green notes.

Cabernet Franc is gaining attention well beyond France.
Argentina's Cabernet Franc from the Valle de Uco has become one of the country's most exciting new wines, rivalling Malbec for critics' attention.
Why does Cabernet Franc suit cooler regions?
It ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon
It doesn't need extreme heat, and it buds earlier, not later.
Cabernet Franc is single-variety in the Loire and blended in Bordeaux

Describe the Loire's Cabernet Franc appellations

In the Loire's Touraine and Anjou-Saumur, Cabernet Franc makes most of the red wine. Chinon, Bourgueil and Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil, in Touraine, and Saumur-Champigny, in Saumur, are the key appellations. The wines are medium-bodied, fresh and perfumed, with raspberry, violet and graphite.

Soils shape the style. Sandy and gravel soils near the rivers give light, fruity wines to drink young. Tuffeau, a soft, white limestone, and clay-limestone on the slopes give more structured wines that can age 10 to 20 years. The same tuffeau was used to build the Loire's châteaux.
Which soil in Chinon gives the most structured, age-worthy Cabernet Franc?
Limestone slopes give firmer, longer-lived wines than riverside sand and gravel.

Loire Cabernet Franc ranges from light, juicy wines, served cool in Paris bistros, to serious, oaked wines from old vines. Rosé de Loire and Cabernet d'Anjou, a rosé often off-dry, also use it. Cooler vintages can show more green notes; warmer ones, riper fruit.
Which are Loire Cabernet Franc appellations?

Explain why it suits the Right Bank

In Bordeaux, Cabernet Franc is about 10% of red plantings. It adds aromatic lift, freshness and fine tannins to blends. On the Left Bank, it's a minor partner to Cabernet Sauvignon. On the Right Bank, in Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, it often plays a bigger role alongside Merlot.

Château Cheval Blanc, in Saint-Émilion, often uses over 50% Cabernet Franc, on gravel and clay near Pomerol. Château Ausone, on limestone slopes, also uses around half. These show Cabernet Franc can make some of the world's greatest wines, with perfume, freshness and longevity.
Cheval Blanc: over half Cabernet Franc
Which Saint-Émilion estate often uses over 50% Cabernet Franc?
Cheval Blanc is famous for its high share of Cabernet Franc.

The Right Bank's cooler clay and limestone suit early-ripening grapes. Cabernet Franc ripens before Cabernet Sauvignon, so it does well there. Limestone slopes give it freshness and structure, complementing Merlot's plumpness.
Cabernet Franc is the most planted grape in Bordeaux.
Not true. Merlot is the most planted. Cabernet Franc is about 10%.
Cabernet Franc adds lift and freshness to Bordeaux blends
Cheval Blanc and Ausone use a high share
It suits the Right Bank's cooler soils

Cabernet Franc's fresh acidity and moderate tannin make it food-friendly. Light Loire styles suit charcuterie, pork rillettes, roast chicken and goat's cheese. Fuller styles suit lamb, duck and dishes with herbs and roasted peppers, which echo its own green notes.

Serve light Loire Cabernet Franc slightly cool, about 14 to 15 degrees. Fuller versions at 16 to 17. Simple Loire reds are best within three years. Top Chinon and Bourgueil from tuffeau age 10 to 20 years. Cheval Blanc ages for decades.
Why does Cabernet Franc suit dishes with herbs and roasted peppers?
They echo its own leafy notes
Herbal food echoes the wine's leafy, green side.
Try a young Chinon slightly chilled with pork rillettes on bread. It's a classic Loire combination.
